passage:
The concept of "moral hazard"—that is, the tendency of insurance or other protective arrangements to encourage the very risky behavior they are designed to guard against—has migrated from its origins in actuarial science into the broader discourse of political economy. Economists and political theorists now debate whether welfare states systematically generate moral hazard at the level of national institutions, not merely individual behavior. Three competing accounts of this phenomenon have emerged, and they differ sharply in their diagnoses and prescriptions.

The first account, associated with the economist Friedrich von Hayek and later formalized by Charles Murray in his influential 1984 study, holds that public transfer programs create a structural dependency by altering the cost-benefit calculations of recipients. When the state subsidizes idleness or failure, the argument runs, individuals rationally reduce their investment in self-sufficiency. Murray's empirical claim was stark: U.S. poverty rates, which had fallen by roughly half between 1950 and 1965, leveled off and then rose modestly after the Great Society programs of the mid-1960s expanded federal assistance. For Murray, the coincidence of expanded transfers and stalled poverty reduction was more than coincidental—it was causal.

But the sociologist William Julius Wilson challenged this account on structural grounds. Wilson argued that the timing Murray identified reflected not welfare dependency but deindustrialization: the simultaneous departure of manufacturing employment from inner cities concentrated poverty among those left behind regardless of transfer levels. Wilson's reanalysis suggested that controlling for the loss of low-skill jobs rendered the transfer-poverty correlation statistically insignificant. His account thus separated the moral hazard hypothesis from its empirical anchoring, casting doubt on whether behavioral change, rather than labor-market restructuring, drove the observed trend.

A third position, advanced more recently by the political economist Jacob Hacker, attempts a synthesis. Hacker acknowledges both that some individuals respond to incentives in the manner Hayek and Murray described and that structural labor-market changes of the kind Wilson documented are real and powerful. But Hacker's innovation is to locate the unit of moral hazard not in the individual beneficiary but in the political institutions themselves. When governments offload risk onto households—through pension privatization, reduced unemployment insurance, or the shift from defined-benefit to defined-contribution retirement plans—they actually increase household risk exposure while reducing state liability. This "risk shift," Hacker contends, represents an institutional moral hazard: legislators and executives face incentives to reduce visible expenditures in the short term even when doing so imposes larger but less visible costs on the broader population over longer time horizons. The implication is that moral hazard is not merely a problem of individual incentive design but a structural feature of democratic accountability itself, one that may be self-reinforcing precisely because its costs are diffuse and deferred.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The concept of moral hazard, originally developed in actuarial science, has been misapplied by economists who extend it to welfare state institutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three competing accounts of institutional moral hazard in welfare states differ in their identification of the relevant unit of analysis and in the empirical evidence each marshals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: William Julius Wilson's structural reanalysis of poverty data effectively refutes the dependency thesis advanced by Friedrich von Hayek and Charles Murray.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jacob Hacker's concept of risk shift represents the most persuasive explanation of why welfare states fail to reduce poverty over the long term.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The expansion of Great Society programs in the mid-1960s caused poverty rates to stall, a phenomenon that political economists have struggled to explain.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces three positions—Murray's behavioral/incentive account, Wilson's structural reanalysis, and Hacker's institutional synthesis—and contrasts their units of analysis and empirical bases. Choice B captures this structure across the full passage.
explanations.A: The passage does not claim the concept was misapplied; it traces a legitimate conceptual migration and takes all three accounts seriously.
explanations.C: The passage presents Wilson as challenging Murray but does not endorse the view that he definitively refutes the dependency thesis.
explanations.D: The author presents Hacker's view as a synthesis and innovation but does not explicitly endorse it as most persuasive, and the passage is not specifically about long-term poverty reduction failure.
explanations.E: This accurately describes Murray's claim but is only one account within the passage, not its main point—a paragraph-level restatement trap.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A concept is defined; a scholarly controversy about its applicability is introduced; a resolution is proposed and endorsed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A concept is introduced and contextualized; a first account of a phenomenon is presented; a structural challenge to that account is offered; a synthesis incorporating elements of both is described.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historical puzzle is identified; two incompatible explanations are presented; the limitations of both are detailed; a new puzzle is introduced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A theoretical concept is defined; its application to a specific case is illustrated; competing applications are compared; the strongest application is selected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two scholarly positions are contrasted; a third position that draws on both is introduced; an objection to the third position is raised; the objection is rejected.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines moral hazard and contextualizes the debate. Paragraph 2 presents Murray's behavioral account. Paragraph 3 presents Wilson's structural challenge. Paragraph 4 presents Hacker's synthesis. Choice B tracks this four-paragraph progression accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not explicitly endorse a resolution; the author presents Hacker's synthesis descriptively, not as an endorsed conclusion.
explanations.C: The passage does not detail 'limitations of both' prior accounts, and no new puzzle is introduced at the end—a mis-sequencing trap.
explanations.D: The passage does not select 'the strongest application'; it describes a third, synthesizing account without declaring a winner.
explanations.E: The passage does not raise an objection to Hacker's view, nor does it reject any such objection—a plausible-but-unused-move trap.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Charles Murray's empirical argument rested on which one of the following observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Poverty rates in the United States fell sharply after the expansion of Great Society programs in the mid-1960s and then rose once those programs were curtailed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: U.S. poverty rates declined by approximately half between 1950 and 1965 and then ceased to decline—and modestly increased—after federal assistance expanded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The departure of manufacturing jobs from inner cities coincided with expanding welfare rolls in a way that revealed a structural cause of poverty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defined-benefit pension plans were replaced by defined-contribution plans at roughly the same time that poverty rates stalled among working-age adults.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Individuals who received government transfers invested less in education and job training than those who did not receive such transfers.

explanations.correct: The passage states that U.S. poverty rates 'had fallen by roughly half between 1950 and 1965, leveled off and then rose modestly after the Great Society programs of the mid-1960s expanded federal assistance.' Choice B paraphrases this precisely.
explanations.A: This inverts the causal story: Murray argued that programs caused stagnation, not that poverty fell after expansion. The passage also does not mention curtailment of programs.
explanations.C: This describes Wilson's structural account, not Murray's empirical observation—a wrong-scholar trap.
explanations.D: Defined-benefit/contribution distinctions are associated with Hacker, not Murray.
explanations.E: The passage describes Murray's argument in terms of cost-benefit calculations, not specific educational investment data—a plausible-world-fact trap.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that William Julius Wilson would agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eliminating federal transfer programs would cause poverty rates to decline rapidly in industrialized economies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The apparent link between expanded welfare transfers and stalled poverty reduction disappears once changes in the labor market are taken into account.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Individual behavioral responses to transfer programs are the primary driver of long-term poverty trends in the United States.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jacob Hacker's risk-shift thesis correctly identifies the institutional mechanism by which welfare states generate moral hazard.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Moral hazard at the institutional level is a more serious problem than moral hazard at the level of individual behavior.

explanations.correct: The passage states that Wilson's reanalysis 'suggested that controlling for the loss of low-skill jobs rendered the transfer-poverty correlation statistically insignificant.' This directly supports B.
explanations.A: Wilson's argument is structural, not prescriptive. He identifies deindustrialization as the cause; he does not argue that eliminating transfers would reduce poverty—this overreaches his structural claim.
explanations.C: This is precisely what Wilson challenges; it reflects Murray's position, not Wilson's.
explanations.D: The passage presents Hacker's thesis as a later development; no evidence is given that Wilson endorsed it.
explanations.E: This distinction is the focus of Hacker's argument, not Wilson's. Wilson's argument concerns structural economic causes, not a comparison of hazard types.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of the shift from defined-benefit to defined-contribution retirement plans serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kind of policy change through which governments increase household risk exposure while reducing their own visible expenditures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide an example of how individual behavioral responses to incentives drive long-term poverty trends.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that Murray's dependency thesis applies not only to welfare transfers but also to retirement policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why poverty rates stalled after the expansion of Great Society programs in the mid-1960s.

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that deindustrialization displaced the pension system as the primary cause of income inequality.

explanations.correct: In paragraph 4, the shift from defined-benefit to defined-contribution plans is listed alongside pension privatization and reduced unemployment insurance as examples of how governments 'offload risk onto households'—illustrating Hacker's institutional moral hazard concept.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The example is given in the context of Hacker's institutional account, not the behavioral account of Murray—an accurate-content-wrong-function trap.
explanations.C: The passage does not connect this pension example to Murray's dependency thesis; they belong to entirely separate accounts.
explanations.D: Hacker's account is not used to explain the 1960s stall; that is Murray's and Wilson's territory. The pension example is about present-day risk offloading.
explanations.E: The passage makes no such comparative causal claim about deindustrialization versus pensions.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Jacob Hacker's synthesis can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, as evidenced by the author's explicit rejection of Murray's and Wilson's positions in favor of Hacker's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured appreciation for its analytical innovation while leaving its ultimate empirical adequacy open.

choices.label: C
choices.text: skepticism about its claim that democratic accountability is the primary mechanism generating institutional moral hazard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral reportage, since the author treats all three accounts as equally plausible without indicating any preference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: restrained disapproval, since the author believes Hacker conflates individual and institutional levels of analysis.

explanations.correct: The author uses forward-leaning reporting verbs for Hacker ('Hacker's innovation,' 'attempts a synthesis') and elaborates his account at greater length and with greater conceptual richness than the others—signals of measured appreciation. But no claim is explicitly endorsed, leaving empirical adequacy open.
explanations.A: The author does not explicitly reject Murray or Wilson; overstated positivity trap.
explanations.C: The author does not express skepticism; the passage presents Hacker's democratic-accountability claim as a compelling implication, not a doubtful one.
explanations.D: The author clearly gives Hacker more elaborate and favorable treatment than the other two, so 'equally plausible' misreads the author's editorial weight.
explanations.E: No disapproval is signaled; the author in fact treats Hacker's multi-level analysis approvingly.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine Wilson's challenge to Murray's dependency thesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies show that cities which lost the most manufacturing jobs after 1965 also had the highest rates of transfer-program enrollment, suggesting that deindustrialization and welfare expansion were correlated rather than independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Detailed longitudinal data indicate that poverty rates in regions that did not experience significant deindustrialization also failed to decline after the mid-1960s expansion of federal assistance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Research in behavioral economics confirms that individuals generally respond to financial incentives in the manner Hayek described in his theoretical account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jacob Hacker's risk-shift thesis has been adopted by policymakers in several OECD countries as a framework for reforming pension systems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historians have documented that the Great Society programs were designed in part to respond to deindustrialization, suggesting that the two phenomena were causally intertwined from the outset.

explanations.correct: Wilson's challenge rests on the claim that controlling for deindustrialization eliminates the transfer-poverty correlation. If poverty stalled even in regions with no significant deindustrialization after transfers expanded, this directly suggests that labor-market changes alone cannot account for the stall—leaving open the possibility that transfers themselves contributed, which is Murray's claim.
explanations.A: This actually supports Wilson by showing deindustrialization and welfare expansion co-occurred, consistent with his structural account. It does not isolate transfers as the causal variable.
explanations.C: Confirming Hayek's theoretical claim about incentive-response supports Murray's general framework but does not directly challenge Wilson's specific empirical reanalysis of the poverty-transfer correlation.
explanations.D: Policy adoption of Hacker's framework is irrelevant to the empirical dispute between Murray and Wilson.
explanations.E: This would actually complicate Murray's account by making the two variables endogenous, potentially undermining his causal story rather than Wilson's.

passage:
Among the most contested questions in historical demography is whether the demographic transition—the shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates that accompanied industrialization in Western Europe—was primarily driven by economic modernization or by the diffusion of new cultural norms. The debate matters not only for understanding European history but for predicting patterns in today's developing economies, where transitions are underway at widely varying speeds.

The economic interpretation, associated with Gary Becker's 1960 household-production model, treats fertility as a rational choice. Becker argued that as wages rise and children become more expensive to rear to a competitive standard—what he called the "quality-quantity trade-off"—parents rationally substitute fewer, better-educated children for larger families. On this account, falling fertility is a predictable response to rising opportunity costs, and no special appeal to cultural change is needed. The model generates strong quantitative predictions: fertility should fall faster in higher-wage urban areas than in lower-wage rural areas, and the decline should correlate tightly with female labor-force participation, which raises the opportunity cost of childrearing.

The cultural diffusion hypothesis, championed by demographers Ron Lesthaeghe and Dirk van de Kaat in their landmark 1986 study of Belgian fertility data, challenges this economic determinism. Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat found that fertility decline in Belgium began in French-speaking Wallonia several decades before industrialization reached that region at a comparable level to Dutch-speaking Flanders, whose fertility remained high well into the industrial period. This geographic anomaly—a largely agrarian region undergoing fertility decline while a more industrialized region maintained high fertility—could not be explained by wage levels or female employment rates alone. The authors attributed the divergence to the diffusion of Enlightenment secularism from France, which weakened the pronatalist norms of the Catholic Church in Wallonia before economic incentives aligned with smaller families.

A third position, developed by the economic historian Timothy Guinnane, attempts to dissolve the dichotomy. Guinnane's comparative analysis of Irish and German fertility transitions showed that neither pure economic models nor pure diffusion models fit the data well across regions. Instead, he argued for what he called "institutional mediation": local institutions—churches, village councils, inheritance systems—filtered both economic signals and cultural messages, producing highly heterogeneous outcomes even among populations subject to similar economic pressures and cultural influences. A region with partible inheritance, for instance, translated the economic signal of rising land scarcity into dramatically faster fertility decline than an otherwise comparable region with impartible inheritance. Guinnane's framework implies that any monocausal account of demographic transition is empirically inadequate and that the transition's speed and timing in contemporary developing economies will depend heavily on the specific institutional configurations through which economic and cultural forces are mediated.

questions.questionStem: The primary purpose of the passage is most likely to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that Gary Becker's household-production model provides the most rigorous account of the demographic transition in Western Europe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: present and evaluate three competing explanations of the demographic transition, ultimately suggesting that institutional mediation offers the most comprehensive framework.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that the Belgian fertility data documented by Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat definitively refutes economic models of demographic change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: survey scholarly accounts of the demographic transition and explain why the debate remains relevant to contemporary development policy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast the European demographic transition with fertility transitions currently underway in developing economies.

explanations.correct: The passage presents three scholarly positions on the demographic transition (Becker, Lesthaeghe/van de Kaat, Guinnane) and explicitly links the debate to predictions about developing economies in both the opening and closing sentences. Choice D captures both components.
explanations.A: The passage does not privilege Becker's model; it presents it as one of three positions and implies it is insufficient on its own.
explanations.B: While the passage treats Guinnane's framework as the most elaborated synthesis, it does not explicitly 'evaluate' the others as inferior or declare Guinnane's 'most comprehensive'—overstates the author's endorsement.
explanations.C: The passage presents the Belgian data as challenging the economic model but does not claim it 'definitively refutes' anything—an overstated-conclusion trap.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: The passage mentions developing economies in the opening and closing but does not contrast them with Europe—it uses them as motivation and implication only.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the "quality-quantity trade-off" as described by Gary Becker refers to

choices.label: A
choices.text: the tendency of industrializing societies to invest more in industrial capital at the expense of human capital.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the rational substitution of fewer, better-educated children for larger families as the cost of rearing children to a competitive standard rises.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the trade-off between the quantity of goods a household can produce and the quality of education available in urban versus rural labor markets.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the tension between pronatalist religious norms and the economic incentives associated with higher female labor-force participation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the statistical correlation between rising wages and declining female employment rates observed in higher-wage urban areas.

explanations.correct: The passage states directly: 'as wages rise and children become more expensive to rear to a competitive standard—what he called the "quality-quantity trade-off"—parents rationally substitute fewer, better-educated children for larger families.' Choice B paraphrases this accurately.
explanations.A: The trade-off concerns child-rearing decisions, not capital allocation—a plausible-world-fact trap.
explanations.C: The trade-off is not about goods production or urban-rural education availability; this imports irrelevant elements.
explanations.D: This conflates Becker's model with Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat's cultural account, mixing elements of two separate positions.
explanations.E: The passage says female labor-force participation raises the opportunity cost of childrearing; it does not describe a correlation between wages and declining female employment—an inverted relationship trap.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the Belgian fertility data described by Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat were particularly significant because they

choices.label: A
choices.text: provided the first quantitative evidence that fertility decline correlates with female labor-force participation across different language communities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: revealed a pattern that could not be accounted for by economic variables alone, thereby creating empirical pressure for a cultural explanation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrated that Catholic pronatalist norms were more powerful than Enlightenment secularism in shaping fertility outcomes in industrialized regions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: showed that institutional mediation rather than either economic or cultural forces primarily determined fertility rates in Belgium.

choices.label: E
choices.text: confirmed Becker's prediction that urban areas would experience faster fertility decline than rural areas during industrialization.

explanations.correct: The passage describes the Belgian pattern as a 'geographic anomaly' that 'could not be explained by wage levels or female employment rates alone,' creating the need for the cultural diffusion hypothesis. The significance lies in the anomaly's resistance to economic explanation.
explanations.A: The passage does not attribute this quantitative correlation to Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat; Becker's model makes that prediction, and the Belgian data actually challenge economic models.
explanations.C: The finding was the opposite: Enlightenment secularism in Wallonia overcame Catholic pronatalism before industrialization—so this inverts the passage's claim.
explanations.D: Institutional mediation is Guinnane's framework, developed later. Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat's contribution was the cultural diffusion hypothesis, not institutional mediation.
explanations.E: The Belgian data actually challenge Becker's predictions—Wallonia declined before becoming as industrialized as Flanders—so this choice contradicts the passage.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of partible versus impartible inheritance systems in the final paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide a concrete illustration of how a local institutional arrangement can produce divergent fertility outcomes from the same economic pressure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: refute Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat's claim that cultural diffusion was the primary driver of fertility decline in Wallonia.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that inheritance systems rather than economic incentives or cultural norms are the primary determinants of demographic transitions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: support Becker's prediction that fertility should decline faster in regions where land is scarcer and wages are therefore higher.

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why the demographic transition in Ireland followed a faster trajectory than in Germany during the same historical period.

explanations.correct: The inheritance example is given to instantiate Guinnane's 'institutional mediation' concept: the same economic signal (rising land scarcity) produces different fertility outcomes depending on the local inheritance institution, illustrating how institutions filter economic signals.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The example is not directed at Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat; Guinnane's argument is that neither pure cultural nor pure economic models suffice—not that the Belgian study is wrong.
explanations.C: Guinnane does not claim inheritance is the primary determinant; he argues that institutional configurations mediate both economic and cultural forces, with inheritance as one example.
explanations.D: Becker's model predicts correlation with wages; the inheritance example is about how the same economic pressure (land scarcity) produces different outcomes depending on institutional context—this contradicts rather than supports Becker.
explanations.E: The passage mentions Ireland and Germany in passing as sites of Guinnane's comparative analysis but does not compare their respective speeds of transition.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Becker's household-production model can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: strong skepticism, since the passage immediately pairs the model's introduction with empirical evidence from Belgium that refutes it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: neutral presentation combined with implicit qualification, since the model is credited with generating clear predictions but is implicitly shown to be insufficient by the evidence that follows.

choices.label: C
choices.text: reserved approval, since the author endorses Becker's quality-quantity trade-off as a necessary component of any adequate explanation of the demographic transition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: dismissiveness, since the author devotes the bulk of the passage to cultural and institutional accounts that presuppose economic explanations are inadequate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: principled agnosticism, since the author regards all three accounts as equally unverifiable given the available historical data.

explanations.correct: The author presents Becker's model evenhandedly—crediting it with 'strong quantitative predictions'—but then presents the Belgian anomaly as something it cannot explain alone, implicitly qualifying its sufficiency. No explicit endorsement or rejection is made.
explanations.A: The passage does not frame the Belgian data as a refutation; it presents it as an anomaly that challenges the model—overstated-negativity trap.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse Becker's model as a necessary component; Guinnane's framework implies monocausal accounts including Becker's are insufficient.
explanations.D: The author presents Becker's model with genuine respect for its predictive power; 'dismissiveness' overstates the negative valence.
explanations.E: The author does not suggest the accounts are unverifiable; the passage is precisely about what each account does and does not explain empirically.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that Timothy Guinnane would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The demographic transition in developing economies today will follow the same institutional path as the transition in nineteenth-century Western Europe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A rise in female labor-force participation is a reliable predictor of fertility decline across all institutional contexts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The speed and timing of fertility decline in any given region are likely to reflect the particular institutional arrangements through which economic and cultural forces operate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat's attribution of Walloon fertility decline to Enlightenment secularism is correct, but incomplete because it ignores local inheritance systems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fertility transitions in developing economies can be accelerated by removing pronatalist religious norms, as the Belgian case demonstrates.

explanations.correct: The passage states that Guinnane's framework 'implies that any monocausal account of demographic transition is empirically inadequate and that the transition's speed and timing...will depend heavily on the specific institutional configurations through which economic and cultural forces are mediated.' Choice C closely paraphrases this implication.
explanations.A: Guinnane's comparative analysis emphasized heterogeneity, not uniformity across regions; the passage explicitly warns against expecting the same pattern to repeat.
explanations.B: Becker's model makes this prediction; Guinnane's argument is that institutional mediation means no single variable reliably predicts fertility across all contexts.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage does not indicate Guinnane specifically addressed Walloon fertility or endorsed any part of Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat's specific explanation—this is too narrow and not supported.
explanations.E: This reflects Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat's account applied prescriptively, not Guinnane's institutional framework, which would resist single-factor prescriptions.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios most closely conforms to the mechanism of institutional mediation as described by Guinnane in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A developing country's fertility rate declines rapidly after a government campaign promoting smaller families, regardless of whether wages have risen or cultural norms have shifted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two neighboring provinces in a country experience rising wages at the same rate, but fertility declines much faster in the province where land is divided equally among heirs than in the province where land passes intact to the eldest child.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A city's fertility rate falls as female labor-force participation rises, consistent with the prediction that higher opportunity costs of childrearing reduce desired family size.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An agrarian region adopts Enlightenment values through contact with a neighboring secular culture, and fertility subsequently declines before significant industrialization occurs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A country's demographic transition stalls because neither economic development nor cultural change reaches the rural population, which remains isolated from both influences.

explanations.correct: Guinnane's institutional mediation holds that local institutions—such as inheritance systems—filter the same economic signal (here, the same rate of rising wages) to produce different fertility outcomes. Two provinces with equal wage growth but different inheritance systems producing different fertility trajectories is a direct instantiation of this mechanism.
explanations.A: A government campaign is a policy intervention, not institutional mediation in Guinnane's sense; this scenario also specifically excludes wage and cultural channels rather than showing how institutions filter them.
explanations.C: This is a direct illustration of Becker's quality-quantity/female-labor-force-participation mechanism, not Guinnane's institutional mediation.
explanations.D: This closely mirrors Lesthaeghe and van de Kaat's cultural diffusion account (Wallonia/France), not Guinnane's institutional mediation framework.
explanations.E: This describes the absence of both economic and cultural forces, not the filtering or mediation of those forces through institutions—a wrong-mechanism trap.

passage:
The sociology of professions has long debated how occupational groups acquire and maintain the authority to regulate their own practice—what the sociologist Andrew Abbott called "jurisdiction." The classic functionalist account, associated with Talcott Parsons, held that professions earn societal trust through demonstrated technical competence and a service orientation: the public grants autonomy to doctors and lawyers because those occupations reliably deploy specialized knowledge in the client's interest. But since the 1970s, this consensual picture has been challenged by conflict theorists who argue that professional authority is secured not primarily through service but through strategic exclusion—the deliberate limitation of market supply through licensing, credentialing, and scope-of-practice restrictions that benefit incumbents at the expense of consumers and would-be entrants.

The most influential conflict account is that of Eliot Freidson, whose analysis of the American medical profession argued that physicians secured dominance not by demonstrating superior patient outcomes but by obtaining state-backed legal authority to exclude competitors—chiropractors, homeopaths, and midwives among them. On Freidson's account, the American Medical Association's decades-long lobbying campaign culminated in licensing regimes that had less to do with quality assurance than with market control. The empirical question Freidson raised was sharp: if technical competence drives professional authority, one would expect licensing to track measurable improvements in care; in fact, he argued, the timing and geography of medical licensing in the United States correlated more tightly with the economic interests of organized medicine than with any documented improvement in patient outcomes.

Magali Sarfatti Larson extended Freidson's analysis by introducing the concept of the "professional project"—the collective effort by an occupational group to translate a cognitive resource, such as specialized knowledge, into social and economic rewards. For Larson, the key move in any professional project is the standardization of training and the restriction of entry—moves that create market scarcity and thereby elevate both the status and the income of practitioners. Larson's framework illuminated occupations beyond medicine: engineers, accountants, and architects all undertook analogous projects of credential-based market closure during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Yet Larson acknowledged a complication: the success of any professional project depends partly on the state's willingness to enforce exclusions, which means professional authority is never purely self-generated but always co-produced with political power.

The most significant recent challenge to both Freidson and Larson comes from organizational sociologists who emphasize what they call "institutional logics"—the taken-for-granted assumptions about appropriate practice that permeate organizational fields. Scholars such as Patricia Thornton and William Ocasio argue that professional authority is reproduced not primarily through explicit market-exclusion strategies but through the embedding of professional categories in the cognitive frameworks of clients, regulators, and third-party payers. On this view, the durability of professional authority depends less on licensing enforcement than on the degree to which professional categories—"the doctor's diagnosis," "the lawyer's advice"—become unquestioned reference points in social transactions. This account implies that challenges to professional authority may succeed not by dismantling licensing but by introducing competing institutional logics: as algorithmic diagnostic tools gain legitimacy among insurers and patients, for example, the cognitive anchor of the physician's expert judgment may erode independently of any change in formal legal jurisdiction.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The functionalist account of professional authority advanced by Talcott Parsons has been thoroughly discredited by Freidson's empirical analysis of medical licensing in the United States.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sociological accounts of how professions secure authority have evolved from a consensus model based on competence and service to conflict-based and, most recently, cognitive-institutional models.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The professional project, as described by Magali Sarfatti Larson, provides the most powerful explanation of how occupational groups across different industries secure market closure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Algorithmic diagnostic tools represent the greatest contemporary threat to professional authority in medicine and law, as they undermine the cognitive anchors that sustain jurisdictional claims.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Freidson and Larson agree that professional authority is primarily a product of state power, a conclusion that the institutional-logics framework both confirms and refines.

explanations.correct: The passage traces a trajectory: Parsons's functionalist/consensus model is introduced and then challenged by Freidson's conflict account; Larson extends that account; Thornton and Ocasio's institutional-logics model then challenges both. Choice B captures this intellectual evolution across all four paragraphs.
explanations.A: The passage presents Freidson's challenge as influential but does not declare Parsons 'thoroughly discredited'—an overstated-conclusion trap.
explanations.C: The passage presents Larson as extending Freidson and acknowledges limitations of her account; it does not declare her framework 'most powerful'—too-narrow and overstated.
explanations.D: Algorithmic tools appear only at the end of the passage as an illustrative implication; the passage is not primarily about this threat—too-narrow trap.
explanations.E: Freidson emphasizes state-backed exclusion; Larson says authority is 'co-produced with political power.' But the institutional-logics framework actually de-emphasizes state power, so this choice mischaracterizes the relationship between the accounts.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A consensus view is presented and endorsed; two variants of a rival view are introduced in sequence; the consensus view is then reinstated with modifications.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A classical account is introduced; a conflict-based challenge is presented and extended by a related theorist; a more recent cognitive-institutional challenge to both prior accounts is described.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A central concept is defined; its application to medicine is analyzed; its application to engineering and law is analyzed; a definition revision is proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A debate is framed; competing empirical evidence from two fields is assessed; a methodological resolution is reached; policy implications are drawn.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An influential theoretical framework is critiqued; an alternative framework is endorsed; empirical evidence is marshaled in support of the alternative; objections are addressed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces Parsons's classical account and the conflict challenge. Paragraph 2 presents Freidson's conflict analysis. Paragraph 3 presents Larson extending Freidson. Paragraph 4 presents Thornton and Ocasio's institutional-logics challenge to both prior conflict accounts. Choice B accurately tracks this sequence.
explanations.A: The passage never reinstates Parsons's view; no consensus view is endorsed at the end—a plausible-but-unused-move trap.
explanations.C: The passage does not define 'jurisdiction' at length and then apply it to different fields sequentially; Larson's extension covers multiple occupations in one paragraph, and no 'definition revision' is proposed.
explanations.D: No 'methodological resolution' is reached and no explicit policy implications are drawn—a mis-sequencing trap using plausible scholarly language.
explanations.E: The passage does not endorse any single framework; it presents each in sequence and concludes with the institutional-logics challenge without declaring a winner.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Eliot Freidson's empirical argument regarding medical licensing in the United States was that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the timing and geographic distribution of medical licensing correlated more closely with the economic interests of the medical profession than with improvements in patient outcomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the American Medical Association used licensing requirements to exclude chiropractors and midwives on the grounds that those groups demonstrated inferior patient outcomes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: physicians in licensed states achieved measurably better patient outcomes than physicians in unlicensed states during the same historical period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the professional project of standardizing medical training was completed before the AMA began lobbying for state-backed licensing regimes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: market control strategies used by organized medicine ultimately harmed patient outcomes by suppressing innovation in competing health practices.

explanations.correct: The passage states that 'the timing and geography of medical licensing in the United States correlated more tightly with the economic interests of organized medicine than with any documented improvement in patient outcomes.' Choice A paraphrases this directly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage says the AMA excluded competitors; it does not say the stated justification was inferior patient outcomes—this imports a detail not in the text.
explanations.C: This is the opposite of Freidson's argument; he contended licensing did not track patient outcome improvements—an inverted-claim trap.
explanations.D: The professional project concept belongs to Larson, not Freidson; the passage does not describe the sequence of training standardization versus AMA lobbying in this way—a wrong-scholar trap.
explanations.E: The passage does not mention harm to patient outcomes from suppressed innovation; this is a plausible-world-fact trap.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that Larson's concept of the "professional project" differs from Freidson's account in that Larson's concept

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats market closure as a product of state coercion rather than collective occupational strategy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: explains professional authority without any reference to the role of the state in enforcing exclusions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: extends the analysis beyond medicine to show how credential-based market closure was pursued across multiple occupational groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: focuses on the client's cognitive acceptance of professional authority rather than on formal licensing and credentialing mechanisms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats the functionalist account of professional competence as largely correct while adding a political-economy dimension.

explanations.correct: The passage presents Freidson's analysis as focused on medicine; it then says Larson's framework 'illuminated occupations beyond medicine: engineers, accountants, and architects all undertook analogous projects.' The extension across multiple occupational groups is the key differentiating feature explicitly stated.
explanations.A: The passage says Larson's framework depends on 'the state's willingness to enforce exclusions'—the opposite of treating state coercion as the primary driver; this also conflates Freidson's and Larson's emphases.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly states that Larson 'acknowledged a complication' in that professional authority depends on state enforcement—so her account does reference the state.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Cognitive acceptance is the core of Thornton and Ocasio's institutional-logics account, not Larson's—a wrong-theorist trap.
explanations.E: Neither Freidson nor Larson rehabilitates the functionalist account; both are conflict theorists who challenge Parsons.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely mentions algorithmic diagnostic tools in the final paragraph in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that technological innovation is the most effective means by which societies can reform entrenched professional monopolies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide a concrete contemporary illustration of how competing institutional logics can erode professional authority without dismantling formal licensing structures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: show that Freidson's market-exclusion account accurately predicted that non-physician entrants would eventually challenge physician dominance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that the institutional-logics framework is superior to the professional-project model because it can explain technological disruptions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that the state's role in enforcing professional licensing has diminished as digital technologies reduce information asymmetries between professionals and clients.

explanations.correct: The algorithmic-tools example is introduced to instantiate the passage's closing claim: that challenges to professional authority can succeed 'by introducing competing institutional logics' rather than by changing formal licensing. It is a concrete forward-looking application of the institutional-logics mechanism.
explanations.A: The passage does not argue that technology is the most effective reform tool; the example is illustrative of a theoretical mechanism, not a policy recommendation—accurate-content-wrong-function trap.
explanations.C: Freidson's account concerns market exclusion via licensing, not prediction of future technological challengers; this misattributes predictive credit.
explanations.D: The passage does not explicitly declare the institutional-logics framework 'superior'—an overstated endorsement trap.
explanations.E: The passage does not mention information asymmetries or reduced state enforcement capacity—a plausible-world-fact trap.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Freidson's argument that medical licensing in the United States was driven more by economic interests than by quality-assurance goals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: States that adopted medical licensing regimes earliest also showed the earliest measurable declines in infant mortality rates, suggesting that licensing improved care quality.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historical records show that the AMA's lobbying for licensing was most intense in states where unlicensed practitioners had captured the largest market share, regardless of documented patient harm in those states.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Countries with nationalized health systems, where physicians are salaried employees rather than market competitors, also enacted strict licensing regimes during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sociological studies show that licensing regimes in professions other than medicine, such as law and accounting, were also adopted in response to documented consumer harm.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Survey data from the early twentieth century indicate that patients generally trusted licensed physicians more than unlicensed practitioners, even before licensing laws were enacted.

explanations.correct: Freidson's argument is that licensing correlated with economic interests, not with documented quality problems. If the AMA's lobbying was most intense where competitors had the largest market share—regardless of patient harm—this directly supports the economic-interest interpretation and undermines quality-assurance as the driver.
explanations.A: A correlation between early licensing and infant mortality decline would support the quality-assurance view, thereby weakening Freidson's claim—wrong direction trap.
explanations.C: Licensing in nationalized systems where market competition doesn't exist in the same way complicates rather than supports Freidson's market-interest story—this choice is at best irrelevant and at worst mildly undermining.
explanations.D: If other professions also adopted licensing in response to documented consumer harm, this pattern weakens Freidson's general claim that licensing is driven by market control rather than quality assurance—wrong direction trap.
explanations.E: Public trust predating licensing is largely irrelevant to whether the AMA's lobbying was economically or quality-motivated—off-target-claim trap.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the process described in the passage as a "professional project"?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government agency mandates that all bridge designs be reviewed by licensed civil engineers after a series of bridge collapses attributed to unqualified designers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A group of financial analysts forms a professional association, establishes a standardized certification examination, and successfully lobbies state legislatures to require the certification for practice, thereby raising the salaries and status of certified analysts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hospital administrator introduces peer-review committees composed of senior physicians to evaluate the performance of junior staff, thereby improving care quality and reducing malpractice claims.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An insurance company begins preferring algorithmic risk assessments over actuarial judgments, gradually reducing the market for credentialed actuaries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A bar association successfully persuades the judiciary to adopt a stricter standard of evidence in malpractice cases against attorneys, protecting members from litigation.

explanations.correct: Larson's professional project involves an occupational group translating a cognitive resource (specialized knowledge) into social and economic rewards by standardizing training, restricting entry via credentialing, and achieving market closure—raising both status and income. The financial analysts scenario instantiates all three components: association formation, standardized certification, legislative lobbying for entry restriction, and resulting salary/status elevation.
explanations.A: Here the state mandates licensing in response to documented quality failures—the functionalist/quality-assurance logic, not the strategic professional project as Larson describes it.
explanations.C: Peer review is an internal quality-control mechanism; it does not involve market closure or credential-based entry restriction—the defining features of the professional project.
explanations.D: This scenario describes the erosion of an existing professional position by algorithmic competition—closer to the institutional-logics challenge described at the end of the passage.
explanations.E: Protecting members from malpractice litigation is a defensive legal strategy, not a professional project in Larson's sense, which involves proactive credential-based market construction.
